## The magic.table: a recorded-computation table

A `magic.table` wraps a data frame so that `dplyr::mutate()` *records* each
expression as column provenance instead of computing it. The recorded columns
are then **exported as live formulas** to an external table, an Excel workbook
or a Google Sheet. Editing a source cell in the spreadsheet recomputes the
derived columns, because they are real formulas, not pasted values.

```{r magic-table, eval = TRUE}
library(magic.table)
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble::tibble(
  region = c("E", "W", "S"),
  sales  = c(120, 80, 60),
  cost   = c( 40, 30, 20)
)

mt <- df |>
  magic.table() |>
  mutate(margin     = sales - cost,
         margin_pct = margin / sales)
mt
```

Nothing has been computed: the printout counts one recorded op.

### Inspecting column provenance

`provenance()` reports, per column, whether it is an original `source` column
or one `computed` by a recorded `mutate()`, and the expression that defines
it. It is derived on demand from the recorded ops.

```{r provenance, eval = TRUE}
provenance(mt)
```

### Previewing the formulas without writing anything

`as_sheet_cells()` returns exactly the grid a writer would push: original
columns keep their values, computed columns become `=`-formulas anchored at
`start_row` (the header row). No file, no network.

```{r preview, eval = TRUE}
as_sheet_cells(mt, start_row = 1)
```

## Export to Excel

`write_excel()` writes the grid to a sheet of a local `.xlsx`, computed columns
as real formulas. No account and no token: Excel and LibreOffice recalculate
on open, and Google Sheets imports the file with the formulas intact.

```{r excel, eval = TRUE}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
mt <- write_excel(mt, path, sheet = "Sales")
mt
```

The returned magic.table is **bound** to the file (see the `backend` line), so
capture it to keep the connection. An existing workbook keeps its other
sheets, and a re-written sheet keeps its position among them.

## Export to Google Sheets

`write_sheet()` is the same step against a Google Sheet, through
[googlesheets4](https://googlesheets4.tidyverse.org/):

```{r sheets}
library(googlesheets4)
ss <- gs4_create("Q1 sales")

mt <- write_sheet(mt, ss, sheet = "Sales", start_row = 1)
```

The `margin` column ends up holding `=(B2)-(C2)`, `=(B3)-(C3)`, … and
`margin_pct` holds `=(D2)/(B2)`, ….

## Re-writing, and the no-clobber default

Both writers follow one contract. A write to a *new* target just writes. A
re-write to the **same** target first compares the live state (the sheet's
cells, or the file on disk) against the snapshot taken at the previous write.
If someone changed it in the meantime, the write is **refused with a warning**
rather than silently overwriting their edit:

```{r reconcile}
mt <- mt |>
  mutate(margin_share = margin / 200) |>
  write_excel(path, sheet = "Sales")
#> Warning: The target workbook has changed since magic.table last wrote it;
#> not overwriting. Pass `overwrite = TRUE` to write anyway.

# write anyway:
mt <- write_excel(mt, path, sheet = "Sales", overwrite = TRUE)
```

## Extending the translator

The default dialect covers arithmetic, comparisons, logical operators,
`ifelse`, and a small set of math and predicate functions (`abs`, `round`,
`sqrt`, `pmin`, `pmax`, `is.na`). A bare column name becomes the current
row's cell, so whole-column aggregates are not built in. Anything else errors
with a hint pointing at `register_sheet_translator()`, which takes the already
translated arguments and returns a formula fragment:

```{r register}
register_sheet_translator("paste0", function(args, ctx) {
  paste(args, collapse = "&")
})

# a column-wide mean over data rows 2..4 (the header is row 1)
register_sheet_translator("mean", function(args, ctx) {
  col <- sub("[0-9]+$", "", args[[1]])
  sprintf("AVERAGE(%s$2:%s$4)", col, col)
})
```

## Eager summary tables

The original helpers compute nothing lazily; they write a data block flanked
by live-formula summary rows (sums, means, …) to a Google Sheet:

```{r analytical}
write_analytical_table(
  ss,
  df,
  sheet     = "Summary",
  title     = "Q1 Sales by Region",
  summaries = c(Total = "SUM", Average = "AVERAGE")
)
```

The sheet ends up laid out as: title in row 1, a blank row, headers in row 3,
the data, then one `=SUM(...)` / `=AVERAGE(...)` row per summary. By default
every numeric column is summarized; pass `cols` to restrict.

For other layouts, drop a level: `make_summary_row()` returns the one-row
tibble of formulas and you place it yourself, and `col_letter()` turns a
column index into its A1 letter (`col_letter(28)` is `"AB"`).

```{r compose}
totals <- make_summary_row(df, data_start_row = 2, label = "Total", fn = "SUM")
sheet_append(ss, totals, sheet = "Sales")
```
